summary:
GC content is the share of guanine and cytosine in a sequence, and it predicts melting temperature, PCR difficulty, codon bias and even the organism a sequence came from. It returns GC content, AT content, sequence length and estimated Tm (GC rule), and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator takes counts or a raw sequence and returns GC content, AT content and the expected Tm. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the GC Content
sections.html:
GC content (%) = (G + C) ÷ (A + T + G + C) × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
G, C, A, Tbase countsnt
GC contentshare of G and C%

sections.title: How do I use the GC Content?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: guanine (g) of 220, cytosine (c) of 180, adenine (a) of 300, thymine (t) of 300.

Substituting them into the formula gives gc content of 40%, at content of 60%, sequence length of 1,000 nt, estimated tm (gc rule) of 80.63°C.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
30 – 50%AT-richlower Tm; may need additives or a lower annealing temperature
50 – 60%Typicalmost genomes and most successful primers
above 60%GC-richsecondary structure and hairpins; consider DMSO or betaine

  • Human DNA averages about 41% GC; bacterial genomes range from 25% to 75%, and the number is often used to identify an organism from a genome assembly.

  • GC-rich templates form secondary structure that blocks polymerase processivity, which is why they need higher denaturation temperatures or cosolvents.

  • For primers, aim for 40–60% GC and check that the 3′ end is not a GC clamp of more than three bases.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Counting Ns or ambiguous bases as AT.
  • Computing GC content on the coding strand with a counting error introduced by line breaks.
  • Assuming 50% GC means an average primer — a 30-mer and a 15-mer at 50% have very different Tms.

faq.q: What is a good GC content for a primer?
faq.a: 40–60%, with a Tm matched to its partner.

faq.q: How does GC content affect sequencing?
faq.a: GC-rich regions sequence poorly because of secondary structure and polymerase stalling.

faq.q: What does the GC Content actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns GC content, AT content, sequence length and estimated Tm (GC rule). Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
